:::{#thm-diagonalizable}
#### Diagonalizable means a basis of eigenvectors

A $p \times p$ matrix $\matr{A}$ is diagonalizable (@def-diagonalizable)
exactly when it has $p$ linearly independent eigenvectors.
Then $\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}$
with the eigenvectors as the columns of $\matr{X}$
and their eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$.

:::

::: proof

Let $\matr{X}$ have columns $\vecf{x}_1, \ldots, \vecf{x}_p$
and $\matr{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p)$.
Column $j$ of $\matr{A} \matr{X}$ is $\matr{A} \vecf{x}_j$,
and column $j$ of $\matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}$ is $\lambda_j \vecf{x}_j$ (@def-matrix-mult),
so

$$
\matr{A} \matr{X} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}
\iff \matr{A} \vecf{x}_j = \lambda_j \vecf{x}_j \text{ for every } j.
$$ {#eq-ax-xlambda}

**Eigenvectors give a diagonalization.**
If $\vecf{x}_1, \ldots, \vecf{x}_p$ are linearly independent eigenvectors,
$\matr{X}$ has rank $p$ and is invertible (@thm-invertible-rank),
@eq-ax-xlambda gives $\matr{A} \matr{X} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}$,
and multiplying on the right by $\matr{X}^{-1}$ gives
$\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}$
(@thm-matmul-assoc, @def-matrix-inverse, @thm-identity).

**A diagonalization gives eigenvectors.**
If $\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}$,
multiplying on the right by $\matr{X}$ gives $\matr{A} \matr{X} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}$,
so each column of $\matr{X}$ satisfies $\matr{A} \vecf{x}_j = \lambda_j \vecf{x}_j$ (@eq-ax-xlambda).
$\matr{X}$ is invertible, so it has rank $p$ (@thm-invertible-rank):
its columns are linearly independent, and in particular nonzero,
so they are $p$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-thm-diagonalizable}
#### Building the diagonalization from eigenvectors

The eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ of $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
are linearly independent (@exm-eigenvectors-independent),
so with $\matr{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\matr{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(3, 1)$,
$\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}$, the similarity of @exm-similar read in reverse.
$\matr{J}$ of @exm-eigenspace has a one-dimensional eigenspace for its only eigenvalue,
so it has no two linearly independent eigenvectors,
which is another way to see that it is not diagonalizable.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-distinct-diagonalizable}
#### Distinct eigenvalues make a matrix diagonalizable

A $p \times p$ matrix with $p$ different eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

:::

::: proof

Choose one eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
These $p$ eigenvectors are linearly independent (@thm-eigenvectors-independent),
so the matrix is diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalizable).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-distinct-diagonalizable}
#### A triangular matrix with distinct diagonal entries

$\matr{U}$ of @exm-eigen-triangular has the three different eigenvalues $2$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-1$
(@thm-eigen-triangular), so it is diagonalizable,
even though it is not symmetric.
The converse fails: $\matr{I}_2$ is diagonal, hence diagonalizable,
but has only the eigenvalue $1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-diagonalizable-powers}
#### Powers of a diagonalizable matrix

If $\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}$ (@def-diagonalizable),
then $\matr{A}^k = \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}^k \matr{X}^{-1}$ for every positive integer $k$,
where $\matr{\Lambda}^k = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k, \ldots, \lambda_p^k)$.

:::

::: proof

By induction on $k$; $k = 1$ is the assumption. If it holds for $k - 1$,

$$
\ba
\matr{A}^k
&= \matr{A}^{k-1} \matr{A}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-power, @thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}^{k-1} \matr{X}^{-1}\,\matr{X} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(induction hypothesis, and the assumption)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}^{k-1}\,(\matr{X}^{-1} \matr{X})\,\matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}^{k-1} \matr{\Lambda} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse, @thm-identity)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Lambda}^{k} \matr{X}^{-1}.
&& \text{(@def-matrix-power)}
\ea
$$

A product of diagonal matrices is diagonal, with the products of the diagonal entries
(@def-matrix-mult: entry $(i, j)$ of $\matr{\Lambda}^{k-1} \matr{\Lambda}$ is $\sum_l (\matr{\Lambda}^{k-1})_{il}\,\lambda_{lj}$,
and only $l = i = j$ can be nonzero),
which gives the diagonal form of $\matr{\Lambda}^k$ by induction.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-diagonalizable-powers}
#### A closed form for the powers

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
with $\matr{X}$ as in @exm-thm-diagonalizable and $\matr{X}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\matr{X}$ (@exm-similar),

$$
\matr{A}^k
= \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3^k & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
= \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 3^k + 1 & 3^k - 1 \\ 3^k - 1 & 3^k + 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

For $k = 2$ this gives $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$,
which matches $\matr{A}^2$ in @exm-eigen-shift-power.

:::
